messages.content: Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

# Welcome to Payments

Your first week is mostly reading, and that's deliberate. Money movement is the one part of the product where a bug doesn't just annoy someone, it costs them.

Start with `payments-core`. It owns the ledger, and every other service in our stack eventually talks to it. The thing to understand early is that we never mutate a balance directly. Every change is an append-only entry, and the balance you see in an API response is a projection over those entries. This trips up almost everyone who joins from a CRUD background.

Second, read `psp-gateway`. It wraps the three processors we route through and normalizes their wildly different error semantics into our own status enum. The mapping table in `gateway/status.py` is the most useful file in the repo for building a mental model of what can actually go wrong in production.

By Friday you should be able to answer: what happens when we charge a card, the processor times out, and the customer retries? Ask your onboarding buddy to walk you through it if the code doesn't make it obvious.

Access requests go in the `#payments-access` channel. Get the staging database and Grafana on day one; you'll want both while reading.

Your first week is mostly reading. That's on purpose. Money movement is the one part of the product where a bug doesn't just irritate someone, it takes money from them.

Start with `payments-core`. It owns the ledger, and everything else in our stack eventually talks to it. Understand this part early: we never write over a balance. Every change is an appended entry, and the balance you get back from an API call is computed from those entries. People arriving from a CRUD background trip on this almost without exception.

Read `psp-gateway` next. It wraps the three processors we route through and flattens their very different error semantics into one status enum of ours. If you want a mental model of what actually goes wrong in production, the mapping table in `gateway/status.py` is the file to sit with.

By Friday, you should be able to walk through this: we charge a card, the processor times out, the customer hits pay again. What happens? If the code doesn't make that obvious, ask your onboarding buddy.

Access requests go in `#payments-access`. Ask for the staging database and Grafana on day one, since you'll want both open while you read.

# Welcome to Payments

Your first week is mostly reading, and that's intentional. Money movement is the one corner of the product where a bug doesn't merely irritate someone. It removes money from their account.

Start with `payments-core`. It owns the ledger, and sooner or later every other service in the stack talks to it. Fix this in your head early: balances are never overwritten. Every change lands as a new appended entry, and the balance an API call hands back is computed from those entries. Almost everyone from a CRUD background trips over this.

Then `psp-gateway`. It wraps the three processors we route through and squashes their very different error semantics down to one status enum of ours. If you want to know what genuinely breaks in production, sit with the mapping table in `gateway/status.py`.

By Friday you should be able to talk through this: we charge a card, the processor times out, the customer hits pay a second time. What happens next? When the code doesn't make that clear, go find your onboarding buddy.

Access requests go in `#payments-access`. Ask for the staging database and Grafana on day one, so you have both open while you read.
